novelty.reason: This is a robustness check on the project's own decision threshold (δ for the rung verdict). It is not a finding about learners, belief geometry or observability that an ML or interpretability reader would learn from. The bimodality matters only because the per-cell maxima are taken over a query battery the project designed itself. Under the standard view, hierarchical rungs of coarsening differ by orders of magnitude at short context, with a continuum at the individual-query level. So "δ sits in an empty band" is just what the setup predicts. The claim has also partly collapsed. The sync sweep shows the maxima decay through the band as L grows (0.01377 and 0.00999 at longer L), which gives ±1-bucket sensitivity to a ×2–3 change in δ. As a result, "decision-invariant" holds only at L ∈ {2,4}. The confirmatory adoption of δ rests on fresh held-out laws, not on this sweep. It also raises an adaptive-threshold concern: δ was proposed after seeing the band. The only reader-facing content is that lock-owner queries carry the argmax. That is a detail about Yupana's own world, and it follows from lock ownership being the main hidden variable. At most it belongs in an appendix or methods footnote as a sensitivity analysis for the threshold. It is not a contribution, and the paper must not state the invariance without the L-dependence caveat.
novelty.nearest_prior: Standard threshold-sensitivity or robustness analysis practice. Bayesian wind tunnels (arXiv:2512.22471, 2607.19379) and Dalla Riva (arXiv:2604.05469) already take exact-ceiling and excess-over-Bayes measurement as given, so a gap threshold in an empty band adds nothing methodological beyond them.

findings.claim: The (δ_p, Δ_τ) divergent-class surface has no δ_p plateau. The growth factor between δ_p = 0 and 3·10⁻² ranges from 1.6 to 4954 across cells, and the largest δ_p = 10⁻⁴ jump is 65.9× at (12,2,2) ε=½ r2, where the exact corner is 5e-08. Δ_τ has a stability region: at full precision on the corrected kernel, 7/16 L=2 cells are exactly flat, 12 are within 0.5%, 15 are within 4% and all 16 are within 4.2%; (14,4,2) is within 27%. The resulting proposal: Δ_τ = 0.01, and δ_p frozen as a reporting axis {0, 10⁻⁴, 10⁻³, 10⁻², 3·10⁻²} rather than a scalar. The divergent class is non-empty at δ_p = 0 in every windowed cell. At full context pair_prob is δ_p-invariant up to 0.1.
findings.teaches: Any scalar δ_p would silently set reported prevalence by orders of magnitude. Exact-equality divergence measures window resolution (a knife-edge), so the threshold must be reported as an axis.
findings.corrections: v0.1.1 rewording: 'flat band' became 'stability region'; 10⁻⁴ was added to the axis. sweep-rerun §4: 'exactly flat in twelve L=2 cells' was print-precision flatness (7 exactly flat), and 'within 4%' is 4.11% in one cell; both hold on both kernels. Corrected-kernel pair_prob drift ≤1.47×10⁻³, with class counts changed in 26 of 32 cells. The note's banner 'No corrected-kernel rerun' is stale.

support.problems:
I recomputed every number from the committed raws (docs/c1-tv-sweep-{12-2-2,14-2-2,14-4-2,12-12-2}-raw-2026-08-15.json and -corrected-2026-08-21.json). They reproduce. Four problems remain in how the claim is scoped and what status it is given.

(1) The 65.9x δ_p=10⁻⁴ jump is the largest only at Δ_τ ∈ {10⁻³, 10⁻²}, where I checked it: 65.89x at (12,2,2) ε=½ r2 and 63.8x at r1, the same on both kernels. Over the whole Δ_τ grid it is not the largest. At Δ_τ=0.1 the r1 jump is 88.3x, and at Δ_τ=0.3/0.5 it reaches 10⁴–10⁵x because the δ_p=0 surface there is nearly empty. The claim leaves out the Δ_τ at which the figure holds.

(2) The magnitude did not survive confirmatory testing. held-out-confirmation-v0.1.md scores P5b ("δ_p=10⁻⁴ jump ≥10x") as a FAIL. The fresh laws gave 1.0–2.6x at (14,2,2) and 1.2–2.0x at (14,4,2), and the note says the 65.9x "lives at (12,2,2) ε=½ r1/r2 only, where the exact corner is 5e-8 — a near-empty corner makes any jump large." Its v0.1.1 correction then scores P5 as one conjunctive FAIL, and §6 says the round does "not establish ... any δ_p-jump magnitude". m1-exit-evidence-map-2026-09-01 row 5.3 repeats this: "the prevalence shape along δ_p is unpredicted." The claim is marked "established" with no mention of this failure. The qualitative point, no δ_p plateau so δ_p must be reported as an axis, is still supported by that same failure. The 65.9x is a single-cell in-sample extreme and should not be read as a characteristic size.

novelty.reason: This is a sensitivity analysis of the project's own divergent-history definition: the δ_p and Δ_τ thresholds in the (δ_p, Δ_τ)-divergent class from Part II §5. It is not a finding about learners, belief geometry, or observation interfaces. An ML or interpretability reader would expect threshold sensitivity by default. Pair-counting prevalence under an approximate-equality threshold on a continuous TV distance is not flat at the exact-equality corner, and orders-of-magnitude swings between δ_p = 0 and 3·10⁻² are what the mass-weighted CDF of pairwise TV predicts once there is any spread below 10⁻². Reporting a threshold as a sweep axis instead of a scalar is standard robustness practice, like reporting probe results across regularization strengths. Two things are specific to the instrument: the exact δ_p = 0 corner is computed in Fraction arithmetic, and Δ_τ has a stability region. Neither changes what a reader would take away. They justify a design choice (Δ_τ = 0.01, δ_p reported as an axis) that paper 1 needs to state and defend in its methods or appendix, since a prevalence figure is uninterpretable without it. It is not a result a reader learns something from, so it belongs in the paper only as supporting methodology. One caveat on standing: the numbers in the source note are buggy-kernel. The corrected-kernel figures (7/16 exactly flat, the 4.11% maximum, class counts changed in 26 of 32 cells) come from the sweep-rerun comparison, and the note's 'no rerun' banner is stale. Any appendix table should cite the rerun, not c1-tv-sweep-v0.1.
novelty.nearest_prior: Standard threshold-sensitivity and robustness reporting practice. novelty.reason: The takeaway is that a fixed finite set of fact queries does not capture all the predictive information in the trace, because a scheduler coordinate (the round-robin cursor κ) that no query touches can still shift the next-event distribution. An ML or comp-mech reader already expects this. Causal states and predictive-state representations are defined by distributions over futures, and any finite query set is a coarsening of that partition. So the existence claim is the standard view, not a surprise. What is actually new is specific to the project. It closes a statutory witness (D2 clause b) in the Milestone 1 spec, and it shows the effect is small: prevalence around 10⁻⁸ to 10⁻⁶ of law mass, a TV of about 0.011 that clears Δ_τ = 1/100 by only 12%, and it appears only in a narrow corner (U = T_ep−2, two-record windows, ε < 1, B = 2). A mass that small contributes essentially nothing to any learner loss or probe metric a reader would care about. The held-out preregistration is scored 3 PASS / 3 FAIL, with P6 scored on candidates rather than witnesses, and the v0.1.1 correction withdrew the post-hoc framing of the dual verdict. That process is careful and worth keeping in the M1 exit record, but it validates the instrument's own design (the predictive-rung test adds information beyond the Q1–Q5 fact queries) rather than teaching the paper-1 reader anything new. At most it earns one appendix sentence as a design justification ('fact queries are not a sufficient interface-value measure; we include a predictive test and find its contribution negligible under our laws'). It is not a result. Because the corner is so small, it also does not count as a clean demonstration that the instrument works for the observation gap.
novelty.nearest_prior: Shalizi & Crutchfield causal states (cond-mat/9907176) and Littman/Sutton/Singh predictive state representations: predictive equivalence is defined over future-observation distributions, so a finite fact-query coarsening can miss predictively relevant coordinates. Shai et al. arXiv:2405.15943 also notes belief distinctions that matter for longer futures but not for immediate facts or next tokens.

novelty.reason: The result is a conditional-mutual-information fact that any reader who knows computational mechanics or PSRs would predict. An exposed field (lineage) adds information about hidden state only when the in-window observations no longer determine it. Context truncation removes that redundant evidence, so the field becomes informative for short windows that open late. Under a deterministic FIFO completion discipline, the field is more predictable from the other observations, so it adds less. That is where this finding lands. Each part is what the standard view predicts: the sign of the interaction, the fact that it depends on truncation, and full-context lineage being exactly zero. The frontiers (L <= T_ep-4 stochastic, L <= T_ep-6 FIFO) are exact, but they are specific to the C0b world's allocation timing. They teach nothing that carries beyond this simulator. The magnitudes are small: 0.02-0.085 bits global, and per v0.1.1, 54-63% of the FIFO gain is offset-mixture amplification (anchored 0.0116 vs 0.0293). That shrinks the clean part further. The mechanism split (allocator-label recovery vs issuing-thread order) is internal bookkeeping that confirms the project's own D8 candidate mechanism. No learner is involved, so the result says nothing about transformers against ceilings. At most it is a design-validation witness showing the instrument can make an interface field's value depend on context in a controlled way. It could get one sentence in the methods section or appendix as evidence that the observation-gap axis has non-trivial interaction structure. It is not a finding for an ML/interpretability reader. Closest prior: Siems et al. already show that state-reveal density matters. The exact-ceiling version here only confirms the textbook redundancy intuition.
novelty.nearest_prior: Standard conditional mutual information / redundancy reasoning in computational mechanics (Shalizi & Crutchfield; PSRs, Littman-Sutton-Singh): an observable adds predictive information only when it is not already determined by the other observations. Siems et al. arXiv:2602.14814 is the nearest ML work on how observation density affects state recovery.

novelty.reason:
The claim is that windows starting at reset, where the full state is known, look more observable than windows that start in the middle of an episode. Any reader who knows HMM filtering or computational mechanics expects this. A known initial condition is a delta prior. A window dropped into a running process starts from the stationary or occupation mixture, and it has to synchronize again. Shalizi/Crutchfield's transient vs. recurrent causal states and the synchronization literature predict exactly this dependence on the window law. The Shai et al. mixed-state presentation also starts from the stationary prior for this reason. A reader would not learn that observability curves depend on where the window sits.

What is actually new here is that the project reversed its own earlier generalization ("C1 over-synchronizes, so the ladder collapses along L"). That is a methodological correction internal to the project, with no finding for the field. The note's own §5 frames it that way ("generalization, not measurement, is what reversals hit").

The numbers also argue against promoting it:
- Several adjacent-rung gaps sit just above δ: r1->r2 is 0.012, r3->r4 is 0.014, and at ε=1/2 the gaps are 0.009 and 0.010. Under the house boundary rule these should be rechecked at the finest grain.
- The world is half dead at horizon 32, so the means mix a live world with a dying one.
- Nothing is gated per window apart from one spot check.
- It is a new, non-statutory law.

For paper 1 it belongs in a methods sentence: define every ceiling relative to a stated window law, and note that reset-anchored windows inflate apparent collapse. It should not be a result. If the live-world C1′ census shows a quantitative interface-by-depth interaction that one would not expect (for example, rungs reordering with depth rather than simply spreading apart), that could be reconsidered.

novelty.reason:
This finding is about the observation channel. It says nothing about learners. Once you know what within-bucket shuffling does, most of it follows from the design. If you erase the order of events inside a time bucket, the identity that order carried is lost, here which allocator label went to which request. A lineage field that links requests to labels restores that identity by construction. Neither half would surprise an ML or interpretability reader.

The other results are expected too:
- **Rungs r1-r3 identical to every digit:** those rungs add fields that do not touch the request-to-label binding.
- **Delta_an falls with horizon:** the loss from one ambiguous assignment gets diluted over a longer episode.
- **B=1 cells are exactly 0:** there is no within-bucket order to erase.

So the standard view predicts the direction and the location of every effect. What the reader cannot get elsewhere is the exactness and the method: an observation gap attributed exactly (chain, Shapley and envelope all agree, with envelope width 0) to one named state coordinate, on one interface change, in a structured systems world. Prior art does not do this:
- Siems et al. vary reveal density along one dimension, with no ceilings.
- Shai et al. and the Bayesian wind tunnels have exact posteriors but no interface axis and no per-coordinate breakdown of the gap.

That makes this a clean demonstration that the instrument's decomposition machinery works and gives interpretable, single-coordinate answers. It belongs in the paper as a short supporting example (a figure or table row showing that interface manipulation X costs exactly coordinate Y, and that field Z buys it back). It should not be presented as a finding in itself.

It is weaker still because it carries no learner result: it covers gap 1 only, and the ML reader's interest starts at gaps 2 and 3. Two caveats should stay attached before it is cited:
- The note itself says a Truthsayer pass is still owed for C0b.
- The per-endpoint fields had an offset-pooling correction (v0.1.1; law-level fields are unchanged).

The "exactly 0" envelope width and the all-zero r4 cells are boundary values. House rules require rechecking such values at the finest grain, and I did not re-verify them here.

None of these attributes an observation gap to a named state coordinate under an interface manipulation.

novelty.reason: This result is about Yupana's own configuration: which hidden coordinate of this particular simulator the order channel fails to reveal, under which scheduler epsilon and window law. It says nothing about learners or representations, and its general lesson is what a reader would already expect. Under a randomized scheduler (eps=1/2), the unobserved round-robin cursor carries the order-channel loss. Under a deterministic scheduler with full context, that loss collapses to near zero. Truncating the window makes coordinates redundant, so Shapley or chain attributions stop being unique. Adding lineage information helps only where the window has discarded history. All four follow from basic HMM and filtering intuition and from the known non-uniqueness of attribution under redundancy (Shapley envelopes are standard practice). The exact 1/108-bit wait-queue residue at (9,9,3), unaffected by lineage, is a neat exactness curiosity, but it is specific to one cell of one world and teaches no transferable principle. As an instrument demonstration, one example of exact gap-1 attribution by hidden coordinate with honest envelope widths is useful, and a single figure or a sentence in the methods or appendix could show it. The paper-1 contribution is already the capability itself (observation interface as a variable, with exact ceilings), and the 716-cell census adds bookkeeping, not a lesson. The claims check out against the note (§0-§1 headline, gates) and its v0.1.1 erratum, which leaves every law-level number unchanged. That makes it sound supporting material, but not a finding a reader who knows Shai et al. or the Bayesian-wind-tunnel papers would be surprised by. Recommend appendix or supplementary status, keeping at most one illustrative cell as an instrument demo.

novelty.reason: This finding is an erratum for a bug in the project's own analysis code. D8 artifacts chose table entries by offset alone, so every reset-visible endpoint reported the law-level mean. The general lessons are ones any careful practitioner already knows. A check that looks only at the mean cannot catch errors that keep the mean unchanged. A group-by key has to cover the full identity of what it groups. A tidy ratio shared across conditions, such as 2/T_ep, can be one effect spread out by a uniform prior, which is the usual Simpson-style warning about pooled summaries. An ML or interpretability reader learns nothing new about transformers, belief geometry or observability here. The corrected content is also ordinary, and it is not a learner result. The eps=1/2 excess sits entirely at endpoint T=2 (C = 0.57998 bits) and is exactly 0 afterwards, because the first [DISPATCH, DISPATCH] bucket stays ambiguous until T=4. The 1/108 splits as one bit on mass 1/36 at endpoint 9. These are exact facts about the Yupana kernel's posterior, the kind of thing an exact-filtering instrument is built to produce. They show the instrument can localize ambiguity, but they do not change what a reader believes about any interface, context or learner comparison. The erratum belongs in the provenance trail and in the D8 notes, since the withdrawn claims are corrected there. novelty.reason: This is a standard forward (belief-propagation) recursion over a larger state: the chain on (S_t, last-L projected records) is Markov. Anyone who knows HMMs expects memory to be bounded by the number of distinct (state, window) pairs instead of paths, so the exponential-to-linear-in-T drop is the textbook forward-algorithm result. What it gives Yupi is operational. It adds a third independent exact implementation behind the firewall, gated bit for bit against path aggregation, and it makes the deep-truncation and live-world ladders computable. It also forces the D4 budget unit to change from paths to pairs. None of that teaches an ML or interpretability reader anything new. Taken alone it is not even a demo that the instrument works, because it only computes ceilings and says nothing about learners. The note's own status banner calls it "instrument work, exploratory in status", and the D4 erratum for L = 12 is still owed. The pair count saturating at 9996 and 182938 is also specific to this world: C1' unrolled grows with horizon. So the saturation is a property of this kernel, not a general finding. In paper 1 it belongs in a methods or appendix paragraph ("ceilings computed by an exact forward recursion over (state, window) pairs, cross-validated bit for bit against path enumeration; cost table in the appendix"), not in the contributions list.
novelty.nearest_prior: The standard HMM forward algorithm run on the product state (hidden state x last-L observation window), which is the textbook reduction of a finite-window observation to a Markov chain (Rabiner 1989). findings.claim: The offset term I(U; O_ord | O_shuf) that separates the unanchored from the anchored D8 loss appears only under truncation. In C0b it is positive in 141 cells (120 at B=2, max 0.00059; 21 at B=3, max 0.000037, only at (12,3), (15,3), (15,6)) and exactly 0 at every full-context B=3 cell. In C1 v0.2 it is positive in 94 truncated cells, up to 0.223 bits. The 40 truncated cells with an exactly zero offset term are five laws, (6,3,3), (6,4,2), (8,6,2), (9,6,3) and (10,8,2), each shortened by at most three ticks. In C1 v0.3 it is positive in 27 cells, all truncated, max 0.2096. In every world, no cell has Delta_an=0 with a positive offset term: the prereg's 'order hides only window placement' row is empty.
findings.teaches: Order erasure costs where-the-window-sits information only when the window is cut, and never on its own. Anchoring through TIME_CLASS matters in truncated conditions and is worthless at full context.

Problems with how the claim is stated:
(1) Missing scope qualifier. "The 40 truncated cells with an exactly zero offset term" is true only for truncated B>=2 cells. C1 v0.2 has 516 truncated cells with zero offset once B=1 is counted.
(2) The full-context half is true by construction, not a finding. The prereg defines U = max(0, T-L). At full context every endpoint has T<=L, so U is constantly 0 and I(U; O_ord | O_shuf) is 0 by definition. The anchored and unanchored losses coincide there automatically. So "worthless at full context" is a tautology, not a measurement. Only the truncated half, and the empty delta_an=0 row, are empirical.
(3) "Only under truncation" is not "generally under truncation". In C0b, 155 of 296 truncated B>=2 cells have an exactly zero offset term. They span 22 laws, including windows shortened by up to 12 ticks. The C1 v0.2 pattern (zero-offset cells cut by at most 3 ticks) does not carry over to C0b. v0.3 adds one more zero law, (12,10,2), cut by 2.
(4) The "teaches" line says anchoring works "through TIME_CLASS". In the prereg (E2), anchoring is modeled as conditioning on U. m1-exit-evidence-map-2026-09-01.md lists the TIME_CLASS (anchored) axis as UNBUILT, so nothing here measures an actual TIME_CLASS interface.

novelty.reason: Mostly this follows from the definitions. The prereg (§1) defines the offset as U = max(0, T−L). At full context T ≤ L, so U = 0 with certainty and I(U; O_ord | O_shuf) is zero by construction. The claim that anchoring is "worthless at full context" is true for the same reason, so it is not an empirical finding. Under truncation, U is a real latent, so any competent reader expects shuffling to lose some information about where the window sits. The positive offset in 94 and 27 truncated cells, and the small values at B=2 in C0b, are what the standard view predicts. What is left for the reader to learn is small. First, the offset term is zero in 40 truncated C1 cells. These are laws whose truncation is short, at most three ticks, so again not surprising. Second, the prereg row "order hides only window placement" is empty: no cell has Δ_an = 0 and a positive offset. That is a modestly interesting fact about how this generator is structured, but it is specific to D8's attribution bookkeeping and teaches an ML/interpretability reader nothing general. The exact-zero rechecks and the corrected first drafts are good instrument hygiene. They are not the lesson. Keep it as a supporting line in a methods or appendix table about the attribution split, if anywhere, not as a result.
novelty.nearest_prior: This comes from the project's own definition (D8 prereg §1: U = max(0, T−L), which is identically 0 at full context), together with standard sufficient-statistic reasoning. The closest external precedent is the context-truncation and stationarity treatment of mixed states in computational mechanics (Shalizi & Crutchfield). There, an unknown phase or offset in the observation window is a known source of irreducible uncertainty that disappears once the window is anchored at the process start.

novelty.reason: I rate this project-internal and would not put it in the paper. It is a routine engineering fix. The memory blow-up came from building duplicate objects, and interning plus a compact mass representation fixed it. Any systems or ML reader would expect that outcome. It says nothing about the observation gap, the accessible-representation gap, the exposure gap, belief geometry, or how interfaces and context change what is knowable. The method it describes is also standard software practice: checking a refactor that must preserve exactness by comparing whole outputs and orderings for equality and by reproducing committed artifacts byte for byte. The one related lesson with some general value, that exact-rational posteriors stay affordable at this scale (93-bit Fractions over about 2M entries), is at most a single sentence in a methods or reproducibility appendix. It could back a claim that the (40,8,2) exact-ceiling computation fits on one workstation, but it is not a finding. The Codex corrections (the call count revised from about 80M to 23.1M, the MassT denominators, and endpoint ordering) do not change this verdict. They affect only whether the engineering note is accurate. I did not check the note or the repository myself; this rating rests on the claim as it was summarized for me.
novelty.nearest_prior: None of the listed ML or interpretability prior art covers this. The closest work is standard software practice (interning/flyweight patterns, memoizing pure functions, and equivalence testing by comparing outputs of refactored code), plus the Bayesian wind-tunnel papers (arXiv:2512.22471 and follow-ups). novelty.reason: The substance of the claim is that adding fields to the observation (OBJECT, RELATED, LINEAGE) lowers exact posterior entropy over hidden state. A reader already expects that. If the rungs are refinements of each other, H(S|window) cannot increase as you move up the ladder (conditioning reduces entropy, or equivalently data processing). The only open question is whether each step is large enough to measure, and that depends on this particular world and on the chosen delta. It is not a general lesson. The ML/interpretability reader learns nothing new from 'richer telemetry, less uncertainty.' The same one-dimensional point is already made by Siems et al. (arXiv:2602.14814), who show capability degrading as state reveals get sparser. The per-field attribution (RELATED resolves lock-0 owner, LINEAGE resolves the device request) is a readout of Yupana's own semantics. The fact that r3->r4 clears delta by only 1.13-1.42x matters inside the project, but for the reader it is a caveat. What makes the result worth including is the exactness. The ceilings are computed exactly rather than estimated, and they show the interface variable has four non-degenerate levels at a frozen (T_ep,L,B) in a world that keeps running. That is a precondition for paper 1's interface axis, which is its differentiator from Shai et al. and from wind tunnels, but it is not a contribution in itself. It belongs in the paper as a methods or calibration table, reporting each rung's exact H(S|window) and the thin r3->r4 margin honestly, so that the learner comparisons in later sections are interpretable. It should not be presented as a finding. If the paper made a headline of it, a reviewer would correctly call it the expected result.
novelty.nearest_prior: Siems et al., arXiv:2602.14814 (varying the density of state reveals, capability degrades as reveals sparsen, no exact ceilings). The general principle is that conditioning on finer observations reduces conditional entropy. Wind-tunnel papers (arXiv:2512.22471 et al.) already cover exact-posterior ceilings as a method.

novelty.reason: This is an engineering and governance episode, not a scientific result. Peak RSS for one exact-filtering pass went from 13 GB to 5 GB by interning shared State/Record objects and compacting per-endpoint mass. That is standard memory engineering: memoize or intern repeated objects, use a compact representation. No ML or interpretability reader learns anything about observability, belief geometry, or learner-vs-ceiling gaps from it. The process lessons are sound practice, but they only matter to the project's audit trail: re-price when the priced unit changes, answer a budget refusal with exact engineering instead of loosening the rule, and gate equality against the earlier recursion. The one fact a reader might care about is that the (40,8,2) exact pass is tractable on commodity hardware (about 5 GB, about 9 minutes) with outputs bit-identical to the reference recursion. That belongs in a methods or appendix line on compute cost and reproducibility, not presented as a finding. The disclosure is also procedural rather than substantive: the thirty artifacts were produced on the Sep 6 instrument before enactment. The 'exactness itself is the lesson' exception does not apply. The exactness here is equality of outputs across an optimization, which any correct refactor should give, not a measured ceiling.
novelty.nearest_prior: Standard object interning / hash-consing and memoization in exact-inference and model-checking tools (state-space explosion mitigation in explicit-state model checkers such as SPIN/TLC, and hash-consed BDD/state tables). novelty.reason: The lesson is: in a nearly deterministic world, windows that start at reset let a known initial condition plus the dynamics pin down the state, so interface rungs collapse (every gap is 0). Windows that open mid-episode on a contended, never-terminating world have to synchronize from an uninformed prior, so the rungs separate again. A reader who knows computational mechanics will expect this. It is the standard difference between synchronizing from a known start state and synchronizing from the stationary distribution (Crutchfield and Feldman's synchronization and transient information). Othello-GPT already makes the matching informal point: a complete history from the start leaves no observation gap. That the result depends on which endpoints are sampled is a methodological caveat the paper has to report so its interface comparisons are read correctly. It is not a finding that teaches readers something new. The exact collapse horizons (L*=10/8/2), the 4.8x/11x/1.4x ratios and the at-threshold census values show that the instrument works, but the direction is what theory predicts. The phrase "exit clause reverses" is project vocabulary with no external meaning. Recommendation: include it as a short methods note or footnote explaining why paper 1 evaluates mid-episode or stationary endpoints, not as a result.
novelty.nearest_prior: Crutchfield and Feldman, synchronization to causal states and transient information (Chaos 2003; 'Regularities unseen, randomness observed'), which treats observers synchronizing from a known start state versus the stationary distribution. Li et al., Othello-GPT arXiv:2210.13382, where a full history from the start determines the state.

novelty.reason:
A knowledgeable reader already expects the qualitative claim. Shai et al. (2405.15943) is built on the fact that belief states separate histories whose next-token distributions match but whose longer futures differ. Aswadi et al. (2607.17060) prove that immediate logits are lossy because distinct posteriors can share predictive means. Wen et al. (2609.11132) show internal divergence alongside vanishing predictive KL. Ray/Riechers/Shai say the same thing in prose. So "such classes exist at every rung" teaches nothing new.

What the paper can use is the exact size of the effect in a structured systems world. Divergent pairs are rare as pairs (pair_prob 0.4 to 0.9% at the content rungs), yet they cover 0.61 to 0.76 of law mass, compared with about 0.20 at r0. That size is set by the interface/rung, and the result certifies that the world is non-degenerate: next-token loss alone would badly understate the latent structure, so the later belief-geometry and gap measurements are not vacuous. The finding is a precondition and validity check (the M1 second exit condition). It belongs in a supporting table or in the instrument section, not among the contributions.

Two caveats for the write-up. (1) The finding is tagged gap "observation", but this is really next-step-versus-horizon lossiness. That is the exposure/query-class distinction, so the label should be fixed or explained. (2) The mass/pair_prob contrast depends on the frozen Delta_tau=0.01 and the delta_p axis. Readers will need that stated before they take the 0.61 to 0.76 figure as meaningful rather than threshold-driven.

novelty.reason:
An ML reader already expects the qualitative lesson. If thread names are drawn fresh each episode, an observer that must predict named state has to resolve 'who is who' on top of what the canonical (permutation-quotiented) observer resolves. So H(S|Pi w) sitting well above the canonical ceiling is close to true by construction: the canonical observer is a quotient that drops exactly this label-assignment entropy. It is also expected that the interface/context ladder (r1->r4 steps, thin r3->r4) survives the change of observer, because the relabeling is orthogonal to the content the ladder measures. The finding's own answer to 'bookkeeping or load-bearing' ('load-bearing for identity, ladder not contradicted') is what the standard view predicts.

The one potentially interesting part is splitting the ceiling exactly into an identity part and a content part. The corrections have already undercut it. [rv-8] shows the two terms are not additive (0.5958 vs 1.2567 at r4 eps=1). [rv-11] shows the r0 residual is not pure identity. The 1.26-bit figure is explicitly not claimed as a property of the world, only of eight records. The result is also exploratory under v0.2.9 Clause 3, with locks, devices, request ids and several pattern forms still undischarged. So the exact numbers do not yet carry a clean lesson either.

The per-episode relabeling cost is also already studied: Part I D3 cites the wind-tunnel line (arXiv:2607.19379) for relabeling being fatal when the statistic needs symbol identities. Binding mechanisms are covered in Wu/Geiger/Millière. In the paper this belongs at most as supporting instrument context: it sizes the binding ceiling that held-out-binding evaluation must be judged against. It should not be presented as a result. It could rise to 'novel-as-instrument-demo' only if a learner is later shown to sit at, or measurably away from, this binding ceiling, since the ceiling is exact.
novelty.nearest_prior: Bayesian wind tunnels line (arXiv:2607.19379, as cited in Part I D3), which reports that per-episode symbol relabeling is fatal when the statistic requires symbol identities. More generally, the standard observation that label-permutation (quotient) observers have lower entropy than labeled observers by the label-assignment entropy.

novelty.reason: The lemma says that when token names are drawn uniformly and independently per episode, the posterior over structural state depends on the window only through its equality pattern (with the binding carried as a nuisance variable). That is a standard invariance and sufficiency fact: under a uniform prior over a relabeling group, the maximal invariant (here the equality pattern) is sufficient. An ML reader who knows the wind-tunnel relabeling work, symbol-agnostic in-context learning or plain exchangeability would expect it. They would treat it as the obvious way to define a rename-invariant target, not as a finding. The Fraction-exact checks across all injections and rungs are good engineering, but exactness only confirms a result nobody doubted. The one quantitative by-product that says something about the world is the canonical-versus-corpus entropy difference. It is small at eps=1 (0.10 bits at r1, 0.01 at r3), and the large eps=1/2 r1 gap is partly an artifact of a dropped cursor. The corrections to it (the withdrawn table, the struck commutation claim, the modulo bias, "exclude fields the kernel never writes") are the project repairing its own definitions. The rest of the 'teaches' field is either the standard premise ("tokens are inert and equality is everything") or house hygiene, not something readers would learn. For paper 1 this belongs in methods or an appendix, as the definition that justifies the corpus track being the comparison point for a trained model. It is not a stated result. It only becomes interesting if H(beta|Pi w) of about 2 bits of unrecoverable binding entropy is later shown to shape learner behaviour, and that result would be a separate finding.
novelty.nearest_prior: Bayesian wind tunnels (arXiv:2607.19379), on per-episode symbol relabeling being harmless for relational key-matching; more generally, the classical result that under a uniform prior over a group action the maximal invariant (the equality pattern) is sufficient

(2) The primary number is misstated as P*(Πr | Πw), which is full-window notation. v0.1.2, a same-day correction made before any evaluator code, moved the headline to the prefix position k = L-1. The ceiling is the prefix distribution P*(Πr_{k+1} | Πw_{≤k}), with a per-k curve (k = 1..L-1) as the main deliverable. The full-window table is kept only for probes and targets.

(3) "Structural + naming = raw token excess exactly per window" is too broad. novelty.reason: A reader who knows the ML literature would expect this. Freshly drawn entity names from a pool of about 56 are irreducible entropy by construction. The finding is a design contract with no measurement behind it, so "established" is too strong a status. Its lesson is that you compare KL or excess loss over the exact ceiling, not raw cross-entropy. That is standard practice: Dalla Riva splits CE into an entropy floor plus an excess term; the Bayesian wind tunnels report KL/bits to the exact posterior; Markovian circuit tracing uses excess loss over Bayes; Shai et al. compare to optimal predictive loss. Projecting to pattern level, so that naming entropy (which symbol-relabeling makes unlearnable on purpose) is kept out of the structural gap, is a good and necessary part of the method. It belongs in the paper's methods section, perhaps as one sentence with the numbers: about 19-20 bits of naming per window against a structural range of about 0.2 bits. It is not a result that teaches readers anything. The exact end-of-window probabilities (1/4, 1/3, 1/2, 1) and the exact per-window identity that structural plus naming excess equals raw token excess are bookkeeping for the instrument. The one thing that could be new is the size of the gap: the naming term is about 100 times the structural signal, which warns that reporting raw loss on a binding-heavy world hides everything. That is still what the standard view predicts once names are randomized per episode.
novelty.nearest_prior: Dalla Riva arXiv:2604.05469 (CE = irreducible floor + excess term); Bayesian wind tunnels arXiv:2512.22471 (KL to exact posterior as the metric); Markovian circuit tracing arXiv:2605.20824 (excess loss over Bayes)

novelty.reason: This finding is about evaluation design, not a result, and it teaches an ML or interpretability reader nothing new. The rule behind it is standard practice for next-token models: score the learner at positions it is actually trained to predict, and compare per-position loss against the Bayes-optimal prefix posterior. Shai et al. (2405.15943), the Bayesian wind-tunnel papers and Dalla Riva (2604.05469) all compare against ceilings conditioned on the context. None of them scores a token the model never emits. The v0.1.2 correction (dropping the headline from k = L, the record after a full window, to k = L-1) fixes an internal mistake that any reviewer would have caught, so it belongs in the project's ledger. novelty.reason:
The finding is that revealing which actor moved is worth far more than any content field. In a scheduler world, a kind-only trace hides the scheduling decision itself, which adds on the order of log2(#threads) bits per step to the posterior over who holds what. Adding the actor name should therefore cut state entropy by much more than refining the content fields of an already-attributed event. An ML or interpretability reader, and anyone who knows partial-observability or causal-state accounting, would predict the direction, and a rough per-event log2(4) estimate predicts the order of magnitude too.

The exact numbers are 1.08 bits max statutory gap, a 3.35-bit H(S) step, and 7.5x the ladder's range. They make a nice calibration row for the observation-gap table, but the exactness does not change the lesson. The note itself says the 1.08-bit step is not decomposed per [rv-9], and the identity-residual check ran on a different law at a different horizon. So the paper cannot yet say how much of the step is identity entropy (a naming artifact) and how much is real who-did-what state information. That is the only version of this result that could teach something non-obvious, for example that most of the step is label entropy that a relabel-invariant learner would never pay for.

The other two parts are project-internal. One is the choice to report r0 beside the exit-clause ladder rather than inside it, and its direction-of-bias argument. The other is the corrected §6 conditional, which bites only at r0. Both are sound governance of the project's own pre-committed exit clause, but they are about the project's decision procedure, not about learned models of computation.

Use in paper 1: keep r0→r1 as one row or sentence in the observation-gap / interface table ("the actor field dominates; content fields are second-order"). Do not headline it. If the identity-residual decomposition is later done at C1' (40,8,2), re-judge that decomposition on its own.
novelty.nearest_prior: Siems et al. arXiv:2602.14814. Their state-reveal density axis already shows that sparser observation removes state information, and that which fields a trace reveals controls recoverability. More generally, standard POMDP / computational-mechanics accounting (Shalizi & Crutchfield) predicts that hiding the controlling action (who is scheduled) costs more entropy than hiding details of an event that is already attributed. The Bayesian wind tunnels (arXiv:2512.22471, 2607.19379) cover the exact-ceiling framing.

novelty.reason: The finding is a set of operating parameters for the instrument: delta, delta_sync and Delta_tau at 0.01 bits, a delta_p axis, and the choice of a sync-horizon estimator. None of it is a claim about learners or about the world. Two methods do the work. The first puts a threshold in the empty band of a bimodal distribution of per-cell maxima, which is standard practice. The second divides a law-averaged entropy by Pr(U>0) so that lossless windows don't dilute it. The finding's own correction states the algebra, H_law = (1-L/T_ep) H_trunc, so dividing by Pr(U>0) is expected bookkeeping, not a lesson. The claim that the dilution matters most at the small T_ep the exact budget allows is also plain arithmetic: when T_ep is close to L, the lossless fraction is large. The frozen-before-the-looping-world point is provenance, not content. An ML or interpretability reader learns nothing from any of this that they would not assume. It belongs in a methods appendix or reproducibility section as a stated choice with its sensitivity axis. The delta_p axis is worth reporting in the paper because there is no common plateau and the pair_prob ratio already reaches 65.9x at 1e-4. That makes it a robustness disclosure, not a result. The core claim holds. I checked the numbers against the sources and they match: 10 splits at (12,2,2) and 121 at (14,4,2); every split differs only in lineage fields; completion-only splits are exactly zero at both eps, and this was checked mechanically on exact posteriors, so the boundary-recheck rule is met. The I5 + always-visible ACTOR argument that causal matching is empty was found sound by Codex (request-id note v0.3). c1-rung-separation-geometry v0.4 corrected the day-six "habitat thinness" cause to the same structural reason. At (40,8,2) the r3->r4 step is 0.0142 / 0.0113, carried by Q3[D0] (exit-clause note §3/§4). No prefix-subset or inert-variable violation. No later note retracts the claim, and I found no recorded decision (the "allocator rung" relabel appears only in the design note). Problems with the claim as stated:

(1) Overreach on B. The claim says "fold request ids into D3 renaming (then r4 collapses into r3 on the id-quotiented target)". v0.3 limits the exact collapse to random ids, with request-id identity quotiented out of both the target and the query suite. It restates B more weakly: r4's *non-allocator* cargo equals r3's. D3 renaming as actually built (learner-corpus-generator-design-v0.1.md §3: "request ids are renamed per episode like the rest (the kernel's lowest-free allocation is structural; its surface name is not)") is a per-episode injection. That keeps the equality pattern among ids inside a window, and under lowest-free allocation that pattern can still carry allocator-occupancy information. The collapse under per-episode renaming has never been measured: the corpus-track note §5 says request ids are not renamed there and Q3 has no pattern form yet (owed under v0.2.9 Clause 3). So the collapse is a hypothesis, not a finding.

(2) "All issue-lineage" / "100% leak share" is loose. c1-rung-separation-geometry v0.2 refinement 2 says "100% lineage-on-IO_ISSUE" is a causal statement, not a field census. About 60.6% (eps=1) / 62.2% (eps=1/2) of the r3->r4 gap sits in windows where issue and completion lineage co-vary. What is established: every split contains an issue-id difference, and the completion adds no independent matching information.

(3) The label "allocator state" can mislead. In the D10 C0b truncated-window results (d10-lineage-verdict v0.1/v0.1.1), FIFO lineage gain is entirely thread-level (thrΔ = Δ, "zero allocator-label component", prereg row 2: "lineage informs issuing-thread membership/order"). Under stochastic completion both components are present. Because ids come only from lowest-free allocation, this is still information about allocator occupancy projected onto the in-flight thread order, not matching. So the "only cargo is allocator state" claim survives, but only if "allocator state" means occupancy history, not id labels. The project's own D10 taxonomy draws that line, and an "allocator rung" relabel should say which one it means.

(4) Scope. "Every rung, law and habitat" for the matching zero is proved analytically under I5. The allocator-cargo readings were measured only at (12,6,2), (12,2,2), (14,4,2) and (40,8,2), all on the canonical track, with request ids never renamed.

novelty.reason: This is a construct-validity correction to the project's own observation ladder, and an ML/interpretability reader would not take it as a finding. That a sequentially allocated identifier such as lowest-free, auto-increment or PID reuse leaks allocator and occupancy state is standard systems knowledge, and it is also the usual shortcut or leakage worry that reviewers already raise about identifier schemes. Readers who know Othello-GPT and Shai et al. would expect any token field that is a deterministic function of hidden state to carry information about that state. The structural half of the claim (under I5 plus an always-visible ACTOR, request-to-completion matching is empty because the thread determines the request) follows directly from the project's own invariants. It is not an empirical discovery. The exact counts (121 of 121 splits being issue-lineage, completion-only splits at exactly zero) are good bookkeeping inside the instrument, but the exactness is not the lesson. It only confirms what the design predicts. Paper 1 has two legitimate uses for this: (a) name r4 the 'allocator rung', or fold request ids into D3 renaming so that r4 collapses into r3; (b) add one sentence stating that paper 1 makes no causal-matching claim, because matching needs I5 relaxation, which belongs to paper 2. The general point that an identifier scheme is itself an observation channel could get one methodological sentence in the interface-design section, but it is not a result. Status caveats: the note is exploratory, v0.2 and v0.3 narrowed it (the Q3 versus Q3thr labelling, and 'r4 == r3 only after quotienting id identity from both target and query suite'), no decision by Tony is recorded, and the 2026-09-13 corpus generator already renames request ids per episode. That last point makes the recommendation largely moot for the current corpus, except for the (40,8,2) canonical r3->r4 step (0.0142/0.0113) carried by Q3[D0], which should be labelled accordingly. Cut: at most a supporting methods footnote, not a claim.
novelty.nearest_prior: Standard identifier-leakage and shortcut-learning practice (e.g. sequential IDs and PID reuse revealing allocator or occupancy state; Geirhos et al. 2020 on shortcut features). Within the recorded prior art, the nearest are Siems et al. arXiv:2602.14814 (the density of observation channels in traces) and Wu, Geiger, Millière arXiv:2505.20896 (binding via identifiers). Neither is needed to predict this result.

findings.claim: The training corpus's generative process is the window law itself: one window per episode, endpoint T uniform on {B,...,T_ep}, U=max(0,T-L), RESET prepended iff U=0, five tokens per record (KIND ACTOR OBJECT RELATED LINEAGE), never packed. Pools threads 64, locks 32, devices 16, request ids 32 with reserved slices (8/4/2/4); keyed HMAC-SHA256 Fisher-Yates injection, exactly uniform. Vocabulary 156 tokens. Frozen-law corpora: ten (r0-r4 x eps), train 200k / val 10k / test 10k windows. Gates: byte-determinism, window-law TV convergence at (8,4,2) over 10^6 windows, rendering uniformity, corpus-track reproduction, round trip.
findings.teaches: A Bayes ceiling is a ceiling for a learner only under the learner's own generative process, so the corpus is constructed to be that process and gated against the exact side.
findings.corrections: Ledger 2026-09-15: vocabulary is 156, not 157 (RESET double-counted); pool rule '>= 8x entity count' applies to the pool including reserved slice; §8.3 per-injection uniformity infeasible at 10^5 episodes, implemented as per-position and first-pair chi-square plus exhaustive 5-token test; endpoint draw keyed by HMAC; 'at most 41 tokens' is a maximum. support.problems:
The design and window-law mechanics check out against learner-corpus-generator-design-v0.1.md §2–§8 and its 2026-09-15 ledger: one window per episode, never packed, RESET iff U=0, five-token records, pools 64/32/16/32 with reserved 8/4/2/4, keyed HMAC Fisher–Yates, vocabulary 156. All 20 committed manifests confirm the pool and reserved figures. Four things are misstated or out of date.

(1) The corpus sizes are superseded. The addendum dated 2026-09-18 in corpus-runs-40-8-2-2026-09-15.md widened every test split from 10k to 100,000 windows under the same run keys. All 20 committed manifests show test = 100000. On the same day, learner-first-results-40-8-2-2026-09-18.md §8–§10 found the 200k models data-limited and regenerated all ten cells as 2M-window corpora with new run keys (train 2,000,000, val 10k, test 100k, seed ranges [0,2e6), [3e6,3e6+1e4), [4e6,4e6+1e5)). That note says the 200k sweep "stands as the low-data row of the data axis, not as the ladder". The claim's "train 200k / val 10k / test 10k" describes only the original 2026-09-15 state.

(2) The claim overstates the gates. Gates 2–4 were run only at C1 (8,4,2), in 5 cells: r1, r3, r4 at ε=1 and r1, r3 at ε=½. Rungs r0, r2 and r4 at ε=½ have none. At r4 ε=1 the corpus-track reproduction value is unpinned (g4_hq_pinned null), so gate 4 is not actually checked there. The run note says outright that "no gate is claimed at (40,8,2) itself". Gate 1 (byte-determinism) was first checked only on r1 ε=½, then on all ten corpora at the 2026-09-18 re-generation. "Rendering uniformity" is the per-position and first-pair chi-square plus the exhaustive 5-token test (ledger (c)), not per-injection uniformity on the real pool.

(3) Smaller points:
- The endpoint grid is the bucket grid {B, 2B, …, T_ep}, not every integer.
- "Exactly uniform" holds only under the idealized-key assumption.
- The window is at most 41 tokens (ledger (g)).

(4) Scope of the "teaches" statement: learner-model-vs-ceiling-contract-v0.1.md §1 and §2.2 (corrected v0.1.2) say the model's ceiling is the corpus-track (pattern-observer) ceiling, not the canonical one. A prefix of a window is not a window of the law, so the headline comparison is a prefix ceiling at k = L−1, not the full-window artifacts. The corpus is the window-law process, but the ceilings a learner is scored against are prefix and pattern-track objects built on top of it.

No house-rule violation found. T is drawn from a key that is independent of the dynamics, reserved-slice hits are an exact count of 0, and nothing uses a variable the kernel never writes.
support.corrected_claim:
The training corpus's generative process is the Part II §2(a) window law, sampled. There is one window per episode. The endpoint T is uniform on the bucket grid {B, 2B, …, T_ep} and is drawn with a key, HMAC(run_key, "<episode>:endpoint"). U = max(0, T−L), and RESET is prepended iff U = 0. Records are five tokens each (KIND ACTOR OBJECT RELATED LINEAGE), at most 41 tokens per window at L=8, padded and never packed. Pools are threads 64, locks 32, devices 16, request ids 32, with reserved trailing slices 8/4/2/4 that are never drawn in training; the ≥8× rule applies to the whole pool. Renaming is a keyed HMAC-SHA256 Fisher–Yates injection, uniform under the idealized-key assumption. The vocabulary has 156 tokens.

The frozen law (40,8,2), looping C1′, has ten corpora (r0–r4 × ε∈{1,½}). They were first generated 2026-09-15 with train 200k / val 10k / test 10k windows. Test splits were widened to 100k on 2026-09-18. The same day all ten cells were regenerated with train 2M / val 10k / test 100k under new keys, and the 2M set is the one the learner ladder uses; the 200k set is kept as the low-data row.

Gates 2–4 (window-law TV ≤ 2√(K/N) at 10⁶ windows, endpoint and RESET marginals, per-position and first-pair rendering chi-square plus the exhaustive 5-token test, and corpus-track H(q|Πw) reproduction) were checked only at C1 (8,4,2), in 5 cells (r1/r3/r4 at ε=1, r1/r3 at ε=½). Gate 4 is unpinned at r4. No gate is claimed at (40,8,2) itself. Gate 1 (byte-determinism) was checked on all ten corpora at the 2026-09-18 re-generation. The learner's comparison ceiling is the corpus-track prefix ceiling at k = L−1 (contract v0.1.2), not the full-window statutory artifacts.

novelty.reason: This is a data-pipeline specification with its verification gates, not a finding. The lesson it claims is that a Bayes ceiling binds a learner only when the learner trains on the same generative process the exact side conditions on. Any ML reader already knows this: Bayes-optimal loss is defined relative to the data distribution. The Bayesian wind-tunnel papers (arXiv:2512.22471 and related) and Shai et al. (arXiv:2405.15943) already train on the exact process whose posterior they compute. The concrete choices (one window per episode, a uniform endpoint, RESET prepended iff U=0, no packing, HMAC-keyed Fisher-Yates identifier injection, pool sizes, a 156-token vocabulary, byte-determinism and TV-convergence gates) are good engineering. They matter to the paper's validity and to reproducibility, but they teach the reader nothing. The one design point with some content is that packing, or training an episode LM and applying the window law only at evaluation (Approach C, ruled out by Part II §2(a)), would silently change which posterior the ceiling refers to. Practitioners already know that train/eval distribution mismatch invalidates a ceiling. So this belongs in the methods section or an appendix, as the construction that makes the ceilings legitimate. It is not a contribution. The recorded corrections (vocabulary 156, not 157; chi-square substituted for the infeasible per-injection uniformity test) are bookkeeping and do not change this verdict.
novelty.nearest_prior: Bayesian wind tunnels (arXiv:2512.22471, 2607.19379, 2512.23752) and Shai et al. arXiv:2405.15943: learners trained directly on the exact generative process whose posterior is computed, so the ceiling is matched to the training distribution by construction.

findings.claim: At 2M windows (d=128, 5 epochs, 3 seeds) the learner-side structural excess at k=7 does not follow the exact side's monotone ceiling ladder. At eps=1: r0 0.005 < r1 0.060 ~ r3 0.059 < r4 0.085 < r2 0.096. r3 is no worse than r1 (sd 0.001 and 0.007, resolved). r2 is above both (sd 0.021; pooled se 0.012; resolved at two standard errors, not three). Exposing OBJECT (r1->r2) makes the learner worse; adding RELATED (r2->r3) brings it back to r1's level. 'The interface that helps the Bayesian observer most per bit is not the one the learner handles best.'
findings.teaches: Whether an interface helps the exact observer and whether it helps a finite learner are different questions: here the learner-side ladder over interfaces is non-monotone even though the exact ceilings fall monotonically down the same ladder.
findings.corrections: Strengthened later in the same note. §14 (six seeds at r2 and r4, eps=1): 'r2 > r1 ≈ r3 is resolved without the outlier'. The lowest r2 seed (0.074) is above the highest r1 seed (0.064) and the highest r3 seed (0.061); r2 mean is 0.086 ± 0.017 over six seeds (0.080, sd 0.006 without seed 3). r4 becomes a mixture at 0.076 ± 0.030 (§14.2). §20: at eps=1/2 the same order holds in the mean (r0 0.005 < r1 0.089 ~ r3 0.092 < r4 0.118 < r2 0.124) but not seed by seed.

support.problems:
I could not refute the core claim. Every number checks out against the committed raws (per_k['7'].structural_bits.mean). At ε=1: r0 0.0047/0.0047/0.0048; r1 0.0641/0.0633/0.0516 (mean 0.0597, sd 0.0070); r2 seeds 1-3 0.0790/0.0894/0.1201 (0.0962, sd 0.0213), and over six seeds 0.0864, sd 0.0173, minimum 0.0740; r3 0.0588/0.0606/0.0585 (0.0593, sd 0.0011); r4 seeds 1-3 mean 0.085, sd 0.042, and over six seeds 0.0758, sd 0.0304. At ε=½ the six-seed means are r2 0.1237 and r4 0.1175, and r1 and r3 (three seeds) are 0.0893 and 0.0923. The "two SE, not three" statement holds: the r2-r1 gap is 0.036 against a combined se of about 0.013, roughly 2.8 se. No later note retracts it: §14 and §20 are the newest treatment and later files do not revisit the ladder. No house rule is broken. The average is over every scored window, with no prefix-conditioned subset. No value sits on a boundary. No inert variable is involved.

The claim is misstated in five ways:

(1) Its headline order uses superseded three-seed values. "r4 0.085 < r2 0.096" is stated as an ordering. §14.2 says r4 is a mixture of two basins and that "where r4 sits relative to r2 is not a question with a single answer at this recipe." So r4 < r2 is not established at ε=1. At ε=½ it holds only in the mean (0.118 vs 0.124), with r4's outlier at 0.239.

(2) The standing r2 value is 0.086 ± 0.017 over six seeds (0.080, sd 0.006 without seed 3), not 0.096. The r2 > r1 ≈ r3 separation rests on six r2 seeds against only three r1 seeds and three r3 seeds. §14 shows a cell can have a worse basin the optimizer finds about one time in three, and three seeds could miss one at r1 or r3.

(3) "r3 is no worse than r1 (resolved)" is loose wording. What is resolved is that there is no difference: 0.0593 vs 0.0597, well inside the noise. Neither interface is resolved as better.

(4) The exact-side "monotone ceiling ladder" needs to name its quantity. The state entropy H(S|Πw) falls strictly: 2.096 / 1.717 / 1.526 / 1.506 for r1 through r4. The pattern-observer next-record ceiling H* only falls weakly: 1.377 / 1.359 / 1.292 / 1.292, with r3 = r4 to three decimals (§3.4). r0 is placed "below the ladder" (v0.2.7.1). It predicts a different target, and its H* of 0.999 is lower than r1's, so r0 does not belong in a monotone-ceiling statement.

(5) The whole ladder is for one undertrained recipe: d=128, 5 epochs, lr 1e-3 → 1e-4. §3 notes that validation loss is still falling. §22 shows that 15 epochs improves every width (r1 d=128 seed 1: 0.060 → 0.047). The ladder has not been re-measured at the longer budget, and §14 says explicitly that nothing is known about whether the basins belong to the rung or to the recipe.

The "most per bit" gloss is fair. OBJECT (r1→r2) gives the largest exact state-entropy step: 0.39 bits in H(q|Πw) and 0.379 in H(S|Πw). It is still interpretation, not a measured quantity.
support.corrected_claim: At 2M windows (d=128, 5 epochs, lr 1e-3→1e-4, an undertrained recipe), the learner's structural excess at k=7 and ε=1 is 0.005 at r0, 0.060 at r1 (3 seeds), 0.059 at r3 (3 seeds) and 0.086 ± 0.017 at r2 (6 seeds; 0.080, sd 0.006 without seed 3). r2 lies above r1 and r3 seed by seed: its lowest seed, 0.074, is above the highest r1 seed (0.064) and the highest r3 seed (0.061). r1 and r3 cannot be told apart. r4 (6 seeds, 0.076 ± 0.030) is a mixture of two basins: four seeds sit at the r1/r3 level and two sit high (0.086, 0.133). novelty.reason:
The general lesson, that an interface which helps the exact Bayesian observer need not help a finite learner, is what an ML or interpretability reader already expects. V-information (Xu et al.) makes this formal: usable information under computational constraints can break data-processing monotonicity. Scaling practice adds that excess over the entropy floor depends on task difficulty, not only on the floor (Dalla Riva frames loss this way). The exact ceilings do make the excess cleanly measurable, but they are not the lesson. The lesson is 'excess is non-monotone in interface richness', and nobody would bet against that.

The specific pattern (OBJECT hurts, RELATED restores) could be interesting, but the evidence does not yet license it as a finding:
(1) It has no mechanism. §10(2) and §13 only show where the cost lands (KIND/ACTOR, BLOCK/ACQUIRE records).
(2) It depends on the recipe. At 200k windows the same learner's ladder is r1 0.270 < r2 0.368 < r3 0.377 < r4 0.491. That is monotone in the opposite direction to the ceilings, not the 2M shape. So 'the learner ladder' changes shape with data volume.
(3) The recipe is under-trained. §22.1 shows d=128 r1 falling from 0.060 to 0.047 at 15 epochs, a budget-limited regime, and the rung comparison has not been redone at matched convergence.
(4) The separation holds seed-wise only at ε=1. At ε=½ (§20) only the mean holds.
(5) r4 is a basin mixture (§14.2), so its rung position has no single value.

As written it is a within-project observation about one under-converged recipe. It would become paper-worthy (novel-as-instrument-demo) only if the r2 penalty survives convergence and scale, and gets a mechanism tied to the exact belief structure. An example would be exposed OBJECT adding binding load on ACTOR prediction, shown by the probes in §16–19. Otherwise it belongs in the paper as a caveat that learner excess must be read per recipe, not as a headline.
novelty.nearest_prior: Xu et al., V-information (arXiv:2002.10689): information usable under computational constraints can violate monotonicity and data-processing, so more observed information can be harder for a bounded learner to use. Secondary: Siems et al. arXiv:2602.14814 (learner capability varies with how densely state is revealed in traces).

findings.claim: The learner's structural excess rises with prefix length k while the exact ceiling H* falls (r1 eps=1 ceiling 1.83 -> 2.18 -> 1.84 -> 1.79 -> 1.63 -> 1.48 -> 1.38 bits). At 200k, every one of the 27 content-rung runs is strictly increasing in k; excess is 0.001–0.03 bits at k=1, and the k=7/k=1 ratio is 18–33 (19–33 in the reading text). At 2M the growth persists in every cell but flattens to x5–14; rungs with more visible fields (r3, r4: x5–6) grow least and r1/r2 (x11–14) most.
findings.teaches: Within one window, more evidence makes the exact observer more certain and the learner relatively worse. This measures the proposal's 'context as epistemic access' axis, and the sign is the notable part.
findings.corrections: §10.5 refines §7.2: at 2M the growth depends on the rung. §11 and §22 show the growth also depends on width: d=256 has the lowest k=1 excess and the steepest rise (x27). The note says the ratio could change with more data, more parameters or a different positional scheme; no positional-scheme test is reported.

(1) "The exact ceiling H* falls" contradicts the numbers quoted with it. The ceiling rises from k=1 to k=2 in every one of the ten cells (r1 eps=1: 1.830 -> 2.177; r0: 1.251 -> 1.412; r3/r4: 2.093 -> 2.360; source pattern-ceilings-40-8-2-k{1..7}-2026-09-18.json). (2) At 200k the "18–33" ratio range is over pooled cells and includes r0. Per run the k=7/k=1 ratio spans 14.3–41.4 (e.g. r4 eps=1 seed1 14.3, r3 eps=1 seed3 14.9, r2 eps=1/2 seed2 41.4). novelty.reason:
Anyone who has read Shai et al. or the Bayesian wind-tunnel papers would predict this sign. At k=1 the exact posterior is close to a marginal that any model learns almost for free, so excess near 0.001–0.03 bits is guaranteed. Each later position needs more evidence integrated to reach the Bayes target, so a capacity- or data-limited learner falls further behind as the ceiling sharpens. A falling ceiling with rising excess is the textbook shape for an under-trained approximate filter, not a surprise.

The note's own evidence points the same way. (1) r0, the no-content control, grows by the same factor (x19–26). §7.2 itself calls part of the mechanism "generic to position". (2) Ten times the data shrinks the ratio from x18–33 to x5–14, and a 15-epoch run shrinks the d=256 excess again (§22). That is the signature of under-training, not a structural property of context. (3) Width changes the slope non-monotonically, and no positional-scheme control was run.

The k7/k1 ratio has a near-zero denominator, so it inflates the effect. It should not be the headline statistic. The claim "the sign is the notable part" overstates the case, since the sign is what the standard view predicts.

The one piece with some content is at 2M: rungs with more visible fields (r3, r4) grow least. This rests on three seeds, and r4 has a known outlier-basin problem (§10.4, §14). Its best use is as a caveat inside the interface-ladder result, not as a finding of its own. As an instrument demo, per-position excess against exact per-position ceilings is useful plumbing: a methods figure that shows the decomposition resolving position. The paper should not frame it as a lesson.
novelty.nearest_prior: Bayesian wind tunnels (arXiv:2512.22471 / 2607.19379), which track per-position closeness to exact posteriors; Shai et al. arXiv:2405.15943 on belief fidelity; the general ML practice that excess loss over Bayes in in-context inference grows with the evidence to be integrated and shrinks with data/compute. The note's own r0 control and 2M/15-epoch runs show the effect is largely generic and budget-driven.

novelty.reason:
Checked against §9–10 of the note. The numbers stand and nothing corrects them. But what the finding teaches is that ten times the data shrinks excess loss (above the exact ceiling) by several-fold, and the gap stays nonzero while validation loss is still falling. Any reader who knows scaling-law practice predicts that. It is the ordinary data-scaling behaviour of an under-trained 0.84M model. The exact ceiling makes "about 4% above the entropy floor" precise, but excess loss over Bayes is already a published framing (Dalla Riva; Bayesian wind tunnels report transformers within 1e-3 to 1e-4 bits of exact posteriors). So the exactness here measures the gap more sharply without changing what it teaches.

The finding's real value is methodological and internal to the project. It shows the 200k sweep's interface ladder and the r4 penalty were data artifacts (§9 reading 2). That belongs in the paper as a control that justifies using 2M windows, probably as a sentence or appendix row, not as a result.

Two nearby observations could be interesting, but this finding does not claim them. (1) The learner's interface ladder at 2M does not match the exact observer's ladder (§10 reading 1). That should be judged separately. (2) A seed-set basin survives the extra data (r4 seed 2). That points to optimization, not a lack of information, but it is anecdotal with three seeds; §14/§15 follow it up.

The claim also doesn't separate the representation gap from the exposure gap. Tagging it gap=representation overstates what an output-loss measurement can show.

support.problems:
The excess numbers are right, but the ceilings and the "within resolution" wording are not.

1. The ceiling denominators are on a different base from the excess. The 0.999 and 0.938 bits come from `mean_next_record_entropy_bits` in `pattern-ceilings-40-8-2-k7-2026-09-18.json`. `mean_next_entropy_bits` (`src/yupi/pattern_ceiling.py:82`) takes the law-mass sum of H(P*) over the table classes. I loaded the k7 tables from `~/.cache/yupi-scratch/ceilings`: the r0 table's mass adds up to 0.85, not 1, because RESET windows with T<8 (law mass 3/20, contract v0.1.2) have no k=7 position. So 0.999 is 0.85 × the conditional entropy. The excess, by contrast, is averaged only over the ~85k windows that do reach k=7. On that same set the ceiling is H/M = 1.176 bits (ε=1) and 1.104 bits (ε=½). The raws confirm this independently: `ceiling_token_bits` at k=7 averages 1.1746 / 1.1758 (ε=1, 200k / 2M) and 1.102 / 1.105 (ε=½). The same 0.85 factor should affect the whole ceiling column in §2 (for example r1 1.377 would be about 1.62). I checked the factor only for the r0 tables. The excess itself is fine because the evaluator uses P* window by window. I found no correction of this anywhere in docs/.

2. "Reaches Bayes within the contract's resolution" overstates it. The contract (`learner-model-vs-ceiling-contract-v0.1.md` §~187) sets δ = 0.01 bits as the adjacency threshold, and δ/3 ≈ 0.003 as a target for the between-seed standard error, not for the size of the excess. At 200k the r0 excess (0.015 / 0.018) is above δ and about 20 within-seed standard errors (~0.0007) from zero, so it is clearly nonzero. At 2M, 0.005 is below δ but above δ/3. So "on the ceiling to within the contract's resolution" holds loosely at 2M and not at 200k. Note §3.1 makes the same loose claim.

3. The naming excess of exactly 0 is true in every raw (mean 0.0, sd 0.0). But it is zero by construction, since no fresh entity tokens exist at r0, so the model learned nothing to earn it. It should not be counted as positive-control evidence. On the boundary-value rule: rechecking at the per-window grain gives sd 0, so it is structural, not a rounded value.

4. The positive-control reading needs one qualifier. r0 excess grows with k (×19–26 at 200k, ×9–10 at 2M), and §7 reading 2 says that growth is partly generic to position. So r0 shows the trainer and evaluator are not broken. It does not show the learner integrates long context without loss.

Prefix-only rule: k=7 membership depends on whether an 8th record exists, which is continuation, not prefix. The contract handles this explicitly: the estimator is conditioned on continuation, with a separate end-of-window term. It becomes a problem only through the ceiling normalization in point 1. The inert-variable rule does not apply.

novelty.reason: A trained transformer matching the Bayes posterior on a small finite HMM-like generator is what a knowledgeable reader already expects. The wind-tunnel papers report 10^-3 to 10^-4 bit agreement, and Shai et al. and Ray/Riechers/Shai recover exact beliefs from from-scratch models. On r0 there are no identities, so the binding and hazard machinery that makes the content rungs hard never comes into play, and the learner being near Bayes is the standard prediction. The result's value is methodological. It is the positive control showing that the trainer, the evaluator and the exact-ceiling pipeline are sound, so the 20-50x larger excesses at r1-r4 can be attributed to the content interface and not to a broken instrument. It belongs in paper 1 as a calibration row or a single sentence, not as a finding. Two small points go with that sentence. First, "sits on the ceiling" should be stated as a small nonzero excess (0.005 bits at 2M) that grows with k (x9-10), not as zero. Given Wen et al. 2609.11132, it should also be worded as matching at the level of predictive loss, not as belief identity. Second, the naming excess being exactly 0 at r0 holds by construction, because no entity is ever emitted, so it is an arithmetic check and not an empirical result. It also triggers the rule to recheck at the finest grain: confirm the term is structurally absent, not a rounded small value. The one thing that could interest readers is that the excess grows with k at a similar ratio at every rung, r0 included (§3.1 reading 2). That belongs to a separate finding about context-depth scaling, not to this positive-control claim.

novelty.reason: A per-field split of excess loss is just the chain rule applied to a field-chained record, and the ranking it gives is what a knowledgeable reader would predict. ACTOR is the highest-cardinality field, drawn per episode from a large renamed pool, so it has the most room for excess. Per-episode renaming is known to be the hard part (Part I D3's own cited wind-tunnel result, and the Wu/Geiger/Millière binding work). Tracking which entity holds what (who acts, and the next KIND given ownership) being harder than naming or peripheral detail fits the standard view that entity/state binding is what small transformers struggle with (Siems et al. on state tracking). Calling it a "binding failure in the sense of D3" is an interpretation, not a measurement. The field-level excess does not separate binding from ownership-state tracking, and the later §18–19 exact-KL work is what actually probes which thread. The "teaches" line also overstates robustness. §11's own table has d=256 at KIND 0.091 > ACTOR 0.044, reading 2 there says only "ACTOR or KIND", and §22 shows the ranking inverts off-recipe. So "the same ranking holds across widths" is false as stated, and the result depends on the training recipe. Two things are useful. The exact ceiling lets excess be assigned to a field. Exposing more fields (OBJECT at r2, LINEAGE at r4) raises the excess on *other* fields even though the exact observer gains, which is more interesting but belongs to a separate finding. As written this is a diagnostic that locates where §18–19 should look. It is not a paper-1 result. At most it is one line showing the instrument can localize excess by field.

(2) The KIND+ACTOR spillover is inflated by the outlier seed. That is r2 seed 3, which §13 says pays extra on every kind and §14 sets aside; its values are KIND 0.0346 and ACTOR 0.0637. I recomputed with the committed six-seed r2 raws (seeds 4-6 from 2026-09-21), which the claim does not use.

novelty.reason:
An ML reader would not assume that a finite learner's per-field excess is additive over fields. Showing a richer input makes a fixed-budget model worse at other predictions is ordinary interference, capacity and optimization behaviour: longer and denser windows, a new field to bind, and the same step budget. Non-additivity is the default expectation, not a lesson.

The project's own later sections also narrow the claim. §14 shrinks the r2 penalty to about 0.02 bits per record relative to r1 once the outlier seed is set aside. §13 puts most of that penalty on BLOCK and ACQUIRE records, i.e., lock contention, so the "seeing the lock hurts who-acts / what-happens" story is really a statement about specific record kinds. §22 then shows the models at this recipe were under-trained: d256 improves from 0.155 to 0.070 with more epochs. So the effect may depend on the recipe (budget, learning rate) rather than on the interface.

The exact ceilings make the bookkeeping precise, but the lesson does not depend on that exactness. What does have value is the parent observation from §10 reading 1: the learner's ladder across interfaces is non-monotone while the exact ceilings fall monotonically. That is an interface-axis result worth reporting. This per-field attribution is at most a supporting diagnostic for it. As written, it does not stand as a finding of its own for paper 1.
novelty.nearest_prior: Siems et al. arXiv:2602.14814 (capability changes as state-reveal density varies, with no ceilings), together with the general multi-task interference and under-training literature. Dalla Riva arXiv:2604.05469 already frames excess over the entropy floor per term.

(2) The comparison uses the wrong rung. The claim is about r3 ≡ r4, but §9 tests r4 against r1 because r3 at 2M did not exist yet. novelty.reason: A difference between two conditions that appears in a low-data, undertrained model and disappears with 10x data is what an ML reader already assumes. It is the ordinary reason to compare interface conditions only at convergence or at matched, adequate budgets, which is standard scaling-law practice. The two things that make it Yupi-specific don't change that verdict. First, the exact ceilings certify that r3 and r4 are informationally equivalent (0.38 for both), so the penalty is known to be a learner-side effect rather than a difference in information. That is the instrument doing its normal job, not a separate lesson. Second, the field split puts the extra cost on the other fields (KIND/ACTOR/RELATED) rather than on LINEAGE itself, which is mildly interesting as optimization interference. But the effect did not last. §9.2 of the note calls it a data artifact, and later sections (§14, §20) reduce what remains to seed-level variation at 2M: most seeds match r3/r1, with outliers such as seed 2 at 0.133 and seed 1 at 0.239 at eps=1/2. So the final picture is "a redundant field makes some seeds train worse". That is ordinary seed variance or optimization fragility, not a finding about interfaces. The claim was superseded within the project, and the warning it teaches (don't read learner-side interface effects from undertrained regimes) is basic method. It belongs in the paper at most as a methods footnote or robustness caveat, not as a result.
